source_description: Beginning as a limestone quarry supplying limestone to a nearby cement plant in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania during much of the 20th Century, the industrial decline experienced by the rust belt during the 1960s and 1970s saw the closure of this former quarry in the mid-1970s, which subsequently flooded with a combination of storm runoff and groundwater. By 1980, the quarry had filled deep enough to make it a suitable scuba diving spot, with it opening to the public as Dutch Springs, operated by Stuart and Jane Wells Schooley, with an open water scuba diving facility, aqua park, and adventure course being located on the property around the quarry. The quarry operated until 2022, when the land was sold to a warehouse development, with the former owners being paid millions for the 95 acres of land so a development company could build two massive warehouses on the parts of the property not occupied by the quarry, with a proposal to fence the quarry off and leave it unused. However, due to the high-quality freshwater conditions in the quarry, a movement was started by divers in multiple parts of the Northeastern United States to prevent its closure. The movement succeeded in two local dive shop owners being donated the land by the developer, which will remain open for more limited open water scuba diving, under the name Lake Hydra. This photo was taken on Memorial Day Weekend in 2022, one of the last weekends Dutch Springs was open.
